prompt: What does `mu.Lock()` do when another goroutine already holds `mu`?
hint: Only one goroutine at a time is inside the critical section.

choices.text: It returns an error the caller has to check
choices.why: `Lock` returns nothing. It does not fail; it waits.

choices.text: It waits until the mutex is unlocked
choices.why: Right, and then it takes the lock itself.

choices.text: It panics, because a mutex cannot be shared
choices.why: Sharing among goroutines is what a mutex is for; copying it is the mistake.

choices.text: It lets both goroutines in, one reading and one writing
choices.why: That is closer to an `RWMutex`, and even there a writer is alone.

prompt: `copied.go` called `Inc` 400,000 times and printed `total: 0`, and the race detector would say nothing. Why?

choices.text: The mutex blocked every call, so none ran
choices.why: The calls ran; the program finished. They changed copies.

choices.text: Each call worked on a copy of the struct
choices.why: Right. A value receiver copies `Counter`, mutex and all, and the copy is thrown away.

choices.text: `defer` ran `Unlock` before the increment
choices.why: A deferred call runs when the function returns, after `c.n++`.

choices.text: Four goroutines cannot share one `Counter`
choices.why: With a pointer receiver they can, and that is the fix.

prompt: The tool that reported `Inc passes lock by value` is `go ___`.
hint: It was introduced in lesson 4 of `go`, beside `go fmt`.

prompt: Why does the section recommend `defer mu.Unlock()` right after `mu.Lock()`?
hint: What happens to a mutex left locked?

choices.text: Deferring makes the critical section shorter
choices.why: It makes it last until the function returns, which is if anything longer.

choices.text: `Unlock` is only allowed in a deferred call
choices.why: `count.go` calls `mu.Unlock()` directly, and that is fine for a one-line section.

choices.text: A `return` or panic in between would leave it locked for good
choices.why: Right. Every goroutine that comes after would wait forever.

choices.text: The race detector requires it
choices.why: The race detector accepts either form; `count.go` passed it with a direct `Unlock`.

prompt: Which of these may be held by several goroutines at the same time?
hint: Readers cannot spoil anything for each other.

choices.text: An `RWMutex`'s read lock
choices.why: Right: any number of readers hold `RLock` together.

choices.text: A `Mutex`
choices.why: A `Mutex` has one holder at a time.

choices.text: An `RWMutex`'s write lock
choices.why: The writer is alone, readers included.

choices.text: A `Mutex` inside a struct with a value receiver
choices.why: That only seems to work because every call has its own copy, which is the bug of `copied.go`.

prompt: `cache.go` with no work under the lock took 79 ms with an `RWMutex` and 65 ms with a `Mutex`. Why was the read lock slower there?
hint: What does an `RWMutex` keep track of that a `Mutex` does not?

choices.text: Readers cannot overlap when the work is zero
choices.why: They can overlap; there is just almost nothing for them to overlap.

choices.text: Counting readers costs more than the tiny section it guards
choices.why: Right. Its bookkeeping becomes most of the cost when the section is one map lookup.

choices.text: A waiting writer kept stopping the readers
choices.why: There is no writer in `cache.go` at all.

choices.text: Map reads are not safe under a read lock
choices.why: Concurrent reads of a map are safe; it is a write alongside them that is not.

prompt: A function holds `rw.RLock()`, finds that an entry is missing, and calls `rw.Lock()` to add it before releasing the read lock. What happens?
hint: `Lock` waits for every reader to leave.

choices.text: The read lock is upgraded to a write lock
choices.why: The documentation says an `RLock` cannot be upgraded into a `Lock`.

choices.text: `Lock` panics with a message about recursion
choices.why: There is no panic and no message; that is what makes it hard to find.

choices.text: It waits for itself to leave, and waits forever
choices.why: Right. Release the read lock, take the write lock, and check the entry again.

choices.text: The entry is added and both locks are released at the end
choices.why: The code never gets past `Lock`.

prompt: With 200 steps of work under the lock, `cache.go` took 641 ms with a `Mutex` and 200 ms with an `RWMutex`. How many times faster was the read lock? Round to a whole number.
Which tool does the section recommend when the whole shared state is one counter?

choices.text: A channel to a goroutine that owns the counter
choices.why: It works and was the slowest and longest of the three.

choices.text: An `RWMutex`
choices.why: An increment is a write, so readers sharing a lock does not help.

choices.text: `sync/atomic`, such as `atomic.Int64`
choices.why: Right: one value, one indivisible operation.

choices.text: A plain `int` read after `wg.Wait`
choices.why: Reading after `Wait` is safe; the increments before it, from four goroutines, are the race.

prompt: A service keeps `requests` and `bytes` as two `atomic.Int64` values, updated one after the other. A report reads both and divides. What can go wrong?
hint: Each atomic is indivisible on its own.

choices.text: Nothing, because each update is atomic
choices.why: Each one is, but the pair is not: the report can land between the two updates.

choices.text: It reads one already updated and the other not yet
choices.why: Right. Keeping two values consistent with each other is a mutex's job.

choices.text: The race detector reports both variables
choices.why: Atomic operations are synchronised, so there is no data race to report; the bug is in the logic.

choices.text: `atomic.Int64` cannot be read from another goroutine
choices.why: `Load` is exactly that, and it is safe.

prompt: Match each job with the tool the section's table gives it.
hint: Ownership moves through channels; state stays put under a lock.

pairs.left: handing a value to another goroutine that then owns it
a cache that goroutines read and change in place
a flag that says the service is shutting down

prompt: In `three.go`, why does `withChannel` need no lock around `total`?
hint: How many goroutines ever touch `total` there?

choices.text: Channels make every variable safe
choices.why: Only the variables a single goroutine owns; four goroutines writing one variable would still race.

choices.text: The increments are atomic on this processor
choices.why: `total += n` is an ordinary read, add and write.

choices.text: Only the goroutine that owns it reads or writes it
choices.why: Right: the others send increments; they never touch the number.

choices.text: `wg.Wait` runs before every increment
choices.why: `wg.Wait` runs once, after all the sends.

prompt: Order the three ways of `three.go` from fastest to slowest, as both runs printed them.
hint: One of them was more than ten times slower than another.

prompt: Which of these copy a `sync.Mutex` and so break it after first use? Choose all that apply.
hint: A copy is made whenever a struct value is passed or assigned.

choices.text: A method with a value receiver on the struct holding it
choices.why: Yes: `copied.go`.

choices.text: `d := c`, where `c` is that struct
choices.why: Yes, an assignment copies every field.

choices.text: A method with a pointer receiver
choices.why: A pointer receiver shares the one struct; that is the fix.

choices.text: Passing `&c` to a function
choices.why: That passes a pointer, and the struct stays where it is.

prompt: A map of user sessions is read on every request and written when somebody signs in, about once a minute. Reads hold the lock only for the lookup. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: An `RWMutex`, because reads are the majority
choices.why: Many readers is half the condition; the other half is holding the lock long enough to overlap.

choices.text: A channel to a goroutine that owns the map
choices.why: That is the mutex in disguise the section warns about, and the slowest of the options.

choices.text: A `Mutex`, then measure an `RWMutex`
choices.why: Right. With a single lookup under the lock, the `RWMutex` was the slower of the two in `cache.go`.

choices.text: No lock, since writes are rare
choices.why: One write a minute alongside reads is still a data race, and Go may stop the program for it.

prompt: Every `RLock` on an `RWMutex` is released by exactly one call to `___`.
In the first run of `three.go`, the mutex took 26 ms and the channel 80 ms. About how many times longer did the channel take? Give a whole number.
